title: Print even and odd numbers separately from an array (check `num % 2 == 0`).
shortTitle: Print even and odd numbers separately from an array
keyPoints: The modulo operator % gives the remainder of integer division; num % 2 == 0 means even, num % 2 != 0 means odd.
In Java, the remainder of a negative dividend keeps the sign of the dividend, so -3 % 2 is -1, not 1.
Always test odd as num % 2 != 0, never num % 2 == 1, because the latter misclassifies negative odd numbers.
A single O(n) pass partitions all elements into two lists using O(n) total space.
The bitwise test (num & 1) != 0 is an equivalent odd check that inspects the lowest bit directly.
Returning two lists from a method is cleaner than printing inside the loop, making the logic unit-testable.

s1_definition.oneliner: For each number, if dividing by two leaves no remainder it is even, otherwise it is odd: route it into the matching collection in a single pass.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Modulo operator (`%`)** – returns the remainder of integer division; `num % 2` is 0 for even numbers and non-zero for odd numbers.
- **Negative sign rule** – in Java the remainder takes the sign of the dividend, so `-3 % 2` is `-1`, which means testing `num % 2 == 1` misses negative odds.
- **Robust odd test** – `num % 2 != 0` correctly identifies odd numbers regardless of sign.
- **Partitioning** – one pass through the array routes each element into an evens list or an odds list, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.
- **Bitwise alternative** – `(num & 1) != 0` checks the lowest bit directly, which is equivalent and marginally faster.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India assigns each account a numeric branch-batch id. For a maintenance window they process even-numbered batches on one server and odd-numbered batches on another to split the load. A clerk reads each batch id and drops it into the even tray or the odd tray.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Separating even and odd numbers is a single linear pass where you test each integer with the modulo operator. If a number divided by two leaves no remainder it is even, otherwise it is odd, and you route it into the appropriate collection. The pass is linear time, and the two result lists together hold all n elements, so the space is linear.

In a banking project at National Bank of India, this pattern split nightly batch work across two servers. Each batch carried a numeric id, and even-numbered batches went to one server while odd-numbered batches went to another to balance the load.

The nuance that matters most is negative numbers. In Java the modulo operator keeps the sign of the dividend, so a negative odd number like minus five gives a remainder of minus one, not plus one. If you tested for odd by checking whether the remainder equals one, you would wrongly classify every negative odd number as even. The robust test is `num % 2 != 0`, which correctly identifies odd numbers regardless of sign.

Remember one sentence: test odd as remainder-not-equal-to-zero, never remainder-equal-to-one, because Java's modulo preserves the dividend's sign.
